description: We are Quasaris, a team of five from Arequipa, Peru. We combine project management, sustainability, software engineering, data science, AI, UI/UX design and agtech. Our mission is to bring free NASA data from space to soil, helping farmers choose crops that fit the water they will really have.t the water they will really have.
summary: Quasaris FarmTwin is a free, bilingual web prototype that helps farmers in the Majes irrigation district (Arequipa, Peru) check whether a crop rotation fits the water they will really have, before planting. The farmer marks the field on a satellite map and enters water allocation, irrigation system, soil texture and priorities. FarmTwin then compares the current rotation with example alternatives under 21 years of daily NASA POWER climate (2005–2025), adjusted to the field's altitude with NASA SRTM and computed with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith. It shows water demand, income and climate risk as ranges across years, not single numbers. A time machine replays past years next to MODIS NDVI, and a 3D twin of the farm lets users test dry, El Niño and warmer scenarios. Results are exploratory and need review with local agronomists. FarmTwin supports farmers and technicians; it does not replace them.
details:
The problem. Irrigated farming covers less than 20% of the world's cropland but produces about 40% of its food and uses 70% of the fresh water withdrawn (FAO), so droughts reach the food supply. In Majes, where much of Peru's onion and dairy production is concentrated, the Condoroma reservoir was at 46% in November 2026, irrigation water was cut by 10%, and SENAMHI gives a 42–60% chance of below-normal rain due to El Niño. Rotation choices are often made before anyone checks whether the water will last the whole season.

What FarmTwin does. Six connected screens:

1. My field: locate and outline the field on a satellite map; enter water allocation, irrigation system, soil texture and priorities (save water, income, soil care, lower risk).

2. Compare rotations: the current rotation and example alternatives (including legumes, cover crops and maize–bean–squash associations) simulated over 2005–2025. Water demand, estimated income, a rule-based soil-practice score and climate risk shown as medians with 10th–90th percentile ranges, plus the years in which the water allocation would have been enough. Scenarios that exceed the user's water limit are flagged.

3. Time machine: replays each rotation year by year next to monthly MODIS NDVI (e.g. the 2016 El Niño drought).

4. 3D farm: a digital twin shaped like the field; users paint crops on plots, choose a past year or a scenario (typical, dry, El Niño, +1.5 °C) and see alert cards for frost, heat and water shortage.

5. Calendar and alerts: crop cycles, rotation wheel, weekly frost/heat risk and irrigation need.

6. Recommendations: bio-inputs, nitrogen balance with legume fixation and field devices matched to soil, zone and crops, each with its reason.

The catalogue covers 21 crops. An AI assistant explains results in plain words and is instructed to quote only numbers from the simulation engine.

How it works. A Python/FastAPI engine downloads daily NASA POWER data (temperature, radiation, humidity, wind, rain), runs quality checks and, as an experimental adjustment, blends the POWER cells that bracket the field's altitude using SRTM elevation (via OpenTopoData). It computes reference evapotranspiration with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith, crop demand with FAO-56 crop coefficients, effective rain, frost and heat days, and a yearly water balance against the user's allocation and irrigation efficiency. The ET0 implementation reproduces FAO-56 worked example 18 (3.9 mm/day), and the engine passes 42 automated tests. Every number is deterministic and traceable; no machine-learning model makes the recommendation. MODIS NDVI and SMAP are visual context only, and ISRIC SoilGrids (250 m) is regional model context, not a parcel measurement.

Benefits. Making assumptions and trade-offs visible helps farmers and technicians discuss water, crop choice and climate variability before committing to a rotation. Next step: a reviewed pilot with farmers and technicians in Majes.

Tools. TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19 (installable PWA), three.js / React Three Fiber, Leaflet with NASA GIBS and Esri tiles, Recharts, Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Vercel AI SDK, hosted on Vercel. English and Spanish, mobile first. No field hardware required.

Demo video (30 s): https://youtu.be/Lanw0QLkEto

Live app: https://quasaris-farmtwin.vercel.app/en
